content: The Guidelines on Hepatitis B and C Testing published in February 2017 by the World Health Organization (WHO) provide comprehensive recommendations for the testing of hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV). These guidelines are intended to support healthcare providers, policymakers, and public health professionals in implementing effective testing strategies to improve diagnosis and treatment outcomes for individuals affected by these infections. The publication is protected under a Creative Commons license, which allows users to copy, redistribute, and adapt the material for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation of the work is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guidelines emphasize the importance of accurate testing for HBV and HCV, as well as the need for updating, disseminating, and monitoring the implementation of these recommendations. They also address the treatment of hepatitis C infection and provide guidance on selecting appropriate serological testing strategies, including oneor two-assay approaches. The document includes detailed implementation considerations for HBV and HCV testing approaches, as well as specific recommendations for testing strategies, such as the use of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and HCV antibody serological testing. It also highlights the importance of post-test counseling and services, as well as innovations in diagnostic tools to enhance access to testing. The guidelines were developed with input from a diverse group of experts, including members of the Guidelines Development Group, systematic review teams, and external peer reviewers. The process was led by Margaret Hellard (Burnet Institute, Australia) as the chair of the Guidelines Development Group, with Roger Chou (Oregon Health and Science University, USA) serving as the guidelines methodologist. Numerous professionals from various organizations and regions contributed to the systematic reviews, evidence summaries, and predictive modeling analyses that informed the recommendations. The publication acknowledges the contributions of WHO staff, regional offices, and external collaborators who supported the development and review of the guidelines. Funding for the project was provided by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The guidelines also include annexes with additional resources, such as summaries of global hepatitis health sector strategies, recommendations for the prevention and treatment of chronic hepatitis B and C infections, systematic reviews, predictive modeling analyses, and declared interests of contributors. These annexes are available on the WHO hepatitis website. The document provides a glossary of terms and a list of abbreviations and acronyms used throughout the text, ensuring clarity and accessibility for readers. It also includes a general disclaimer stating that the designations and presentation of material do not imply any opinion on the legal status of countries or territories, nor do they endorse specific products or organizations. In summary, the WHO guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing serve as a critical resource for improving the diagnosis, treatment, and management of these infections, with the ultimate goal of reducing the global burden of hepatitis-related diseases.
